overview.intro: A comic poem in ballad form about a king who is just and placid, an arch built over the main road, and the chain of events that ends with a melon wearing the crown. The unit follows the sequence of blame — chief of builders, workmen, masons, architect — the blind old man’s verdict, the king’s own place in the noose, and the ministers’ expedient, and asks what the poem is satirising: kings, councils, crowds, or the idea that justice can be administered by procedure.

learn.title: The arch, the crown and the charge

blocks.text: The poem begins with a kingly commission and a piece of civic pomp: an arch is to stand over the main road, and its purpose is to edify spectators, to impress upon the public the glory of the reign. The trouble arrives with physical precision — the arch is too low, and when the king rides beneath it he loses his crown. The indignity is constitutional rather than painful, and the king’s response sets the whole mechanism running: taking it as a disgrace, he orders the chief of builders hanged.

The scene establishes the poem’s ironic method. The king is introduced as just and placid, and every subsequent action contradicts both adjectives while appearing to satisfy them: his justice is the reflex of ordering a hanging, his placidity the indifference of a man who does not ask whom he is hanging. The comedy is structural rather than verbal — the reader laughs because the procedure of justice is followed exactly while its purpose is inverted — and this is what makes the poem a satire on administration rather than merely a story about a foolish king.

items: The arch is built over the main road to edify spectators.
It is too low: the king loses his crown riding beneath.
He orders the chief of builders hanged.
Just and placid describes him ironically from the start.
Satire works through procedure followed and purpose inverted.

learn.title: The chain of blame and the architect’s reply

blocks.text: Each person summoned passes the responsibility upward with impeccable logic. The chief of builders names the workmen; the workmen point to the bricks of the wrong size supplied to them; the masons pass it to the architect who designed the structure; and the architect, in the poem’s pivotal exchange, reminds the king that the plans were amended at royal command. The chain is airtight — every transfer of blame is technically correct — and it ends where all such systems end: with the person who set it running.

The council then does what councils do: unable to resolve the question, it escalates it. The wisest man available turns out to be a very old, blind man who cannot walk, and his verdict is the poem’s comic masterpiece — since only the arch can be said to have hit the king, the arch itself is guilty and must be hanged. The sentence is impossible to carry out, which is precisely its function: the procedure needs a culprit it can process, and the demand for a hanging, once made by the crowd, cannot be withdrawn. The chain of blame has taught everyone to point, and nobody has learned anything.

blocks.caption: The chain of responsibility
rows: Only the arch struck the king

learn.title: The noose and the melon: two endings

blocks.text: The poem’s two endings complete its satire. The first concerns the king: a councillor objects to hanging the arch, the restless crowd demands a hanging now, and the king orders that someone be hanged at once. The noose has been set somewhat high, and everyone is measured against it — and the king alone is tall enough to fit. His own decree is executed upon him, which is the poem’s tightest irony: the system he operated without thought operates on him without hesitation, and the just king receives exactly the procedure he administered.

The second ending concerns the succession. The ministers announce the customary rule — the next person to pass through the City Gate will choose the ruler — and the person who happens along is an idiot whose stock answer to any question is a melon. Asked to choose a king, he says melon; a melon is crowned; and the city accepts its new ruler provided that peace and liberty are preserved and nobody interferes with its business. The final note is the poem’s widest: the citizens do not want a ruler so much as freedom from rulers, and in a state where procedure has replaced sense, a melon governs as well as any of the candidates the chain of blame produced.

items.text: The architect’s reminder that the king amended the plans.
items.note: Logic used to return blame to its source — the chain closes on the king.
Procedure selecting its victim by measurement rather than by justice.

learn.title: Ballad form, repetition and how satire bites

blocks.text: The poem’s form is part of its argument. A ballad — narrative verse in regular stanzas, traditionally sung — carries folk associations of plainness and communal storytelling, and Seth adopts it to tell a tale of official folly in the tone of a tale everyone already knows. Regular stanza lengths and a straightforward rhyme scheme create a momentum that carries the reader from absurdity to absurdity without pausing to object, which is how the poem’s logic of blame gets past the reader’s resistance: each transfer of responsibility is delivered in the same untroubled metre as the last.

Repetition does similar work. Repeated formulas — the summons, the reply, the measurement — make the machinery audible, and the recurring emphasis on the king’s justice and placidity becomes funnier with each contradiction. The satire bites because the poem never raises its voice: there is no editorial comment, no denunciation of the king, and no authorial winking. Everything is narrated in the level register of chronicle, and the reader does the judging. For extract answers, identify the repeated element in the quoted lines, say what machinery it exposes, and note how the flat tone converts procedure into farce.

questions.answer: The arch itself is guilty and should be hanged
questions.explanation: Only the arch touched the king, so by the logic of the procedure the arch must answer — a sentence that cannot be carried out.

He confesses to amending the plans
questions.answer: The noose, set somewhat high, fits only his height, so his own decree executes itself
questions.explanation: Justice by procedure selects its victim by measurement, and the system operates on its operator without hesitation.

questions.prompt: The king loses his ________ beneath the arch that was built over the main road.
questions.explanation: The arch is too low, and the royal loss of dignity starts the whole machinery.

questions.prompt: By the customary rule, the next person through the ________ chooses the ruler.
questions.explanation: The ministers fall back on custom when procedure has exhausted itself.

questions.prompt: How does responsibility for the low arch get passed along? Give four stages.
questions.answer: Four stages are: the king first blames the chief of builders and orders him hanged; the chief passes it to the workmen who executed the work; the workmen point to the masons who supplied bricks of the wrong size; and the masons name the architect, who answers that the king himself amended the plans. The council then passes it further still, judging the arch itself to be the guilty party.
questions.explanation: Four transfers in order, with the reason each gives, are required.

questions.prompt: What does the ending of the poem suggest about the people and their rulers?
questions.answer: The ending suggests that the people are indifferent to who rules so long as they are left alone: when the melon is crowned by accident, the city accepts it without protest provided peace and liberty are preserved and nobody interferes with its business, which means they have judged rulers to be irrelevant to their lives. It also comments on the rulers themselves, since the chain of careful procedure produced nothing better than chance, and the ministers’ recourse to custom shows a governing class that has substituted process for sense. Finally, the idiot’s single stock answer — a melon — completes the satire on choice itself: a system that asks any passer-by to name a ruler deserves the answer it gets.
questions.explanation: Three implications are required: popular indifference, the emptiness of procedure, and the satire on choice itself.

questions.prompt: How does Vikram Seth use the ballad form to make his satire work? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The ballad carries an inherited register — plain narrative verse, regular stanzas, rhyme, the tone of a tale told and retold — and Seth uses it to narrate official folly as though it were folklore. The first effect is momentum: stanzas of even length and a straightforward rhyme scheme carry the reader from absurdity to absurdity without a pause for objection, and since each transfer of blame is delivered in exactly the metre of the last, the logic of the chain acquires a hypnotic plausibility that mirrors how such systems actually work — nobody stops because the procedure continues. The second effect is tonal irony: ballads are naïve in manner, and setting a satire in a naïve form produces a gap between what the verse reports and what the reader understands — the poem never condemns, it narrates, and the flatness of chronicle voice makes the just and placid king funnier with each contradiction than any denunciation could. The third effect is structural symmetry, which the regular form supports: the king’s death and the melon’s crowning are parallel endings delivered in the same register, so that the system’s self-destruction and its replacement by a fruit read as two movements of one mechanism. Repetition, another ballad inheritance, does the fourth piece of work: repeated formulas of summons, reply and measurement make the machinery audible, and each return of the formula exposes more of the procedure’s emptiness. The result is satire that bites without ever showing its teeth — the reader, not the poet, performs the judgement, which is what makes the poem persuasive rather than preachy. Answers should quote one repeated formula, one stanza showing the level tone, and both endings, because the form is not decoration here: it is the argument’s delivery system.
questions.explanation: Full marks require at least three ballad features identified with quotations, an account of how the level tone converts procedure into farce, and a judgement about form as the delivery of the satire.

questions.prompt: Who or what is the real target of this satire — the king, the council, the crowd, or the system? Discuss with evidence.
questions.answer: The case against the king is the most obvious. He is introduced as just and placid and contradicts both immediately: he loses a crown and orders a hanging, he accepts each passing of blame without scrutiny, he amends the architect’s plans without considering consequences, and his final decree — hang someone at once — is executed on himself. His justice is reflex rather than principle and his placidity is indifference, and the poem’s tightest irony is that the procedure he administered without thought is administered to him without hesitation. The case against the council and officials rests on their procedural ingenuity: they cannot resolve a question of responsibility, so they escalate it, summon a blind man who cannot walk as the wisest available, accept the absurd verdict that the arch is guilty, and then fall back on the expedient of custom when even that fails. Their sin is not stupidity but the substitution of process for sense — each step correct, the sum ridiculous. The case against the crowd is smaller but real: it is the crowd that demands a hanging once the question is raised, and the crowd that acquiesces in the melon, so public appetite supplies the pressure that the machinery converts into outcomes nobody chose. The case for the system itself is the strongest, because the poem consistently shows individuals behaving predictably within their roles: the king does what kings in the poem’s logic do, officials pass what officials pass, and the custom of the passer-by is an existing rule rather than an invention — no one needs to be very foolish for the result to be folly, which means the foolishness is in the arrangement. The balanced judgement is that the system is the target and the other three are its specimens: the king illustrates it, the council operates it, the crowd feeds it, and the melon is its product. An answer should therefore argue each candidate from specific episodes — the chain, the noose, the gate — and conclude that the poem satirises a form of governance in which procedure has replaced judgement, since that reading explains why the ending is resignation rather than outrage: in such a system, a melon is not an interruption of rule but its logical conclusion.
questions.explanation: Full marks require all four candidates argued with specific evidence, the recognition that the crowd supplies pressure rather than policy, and a judgement explaining why the system rather than any actor is the poem’s true subject.
